cards.title: Adopt a market-driven rather than marketing-driven orientation
cards.summary: Be market-driven by listening to and shaping the market's worldview, instead of marketing-driven and fixated on tactics, offers, and surface polish.
cards.use_when: When setting your store's product roadmap, brand positioning, or overall merchandising strategy and deciding what drives decisions.
steps: Diagnose which force drives your store: chef-, tech-, money-, or marketing-driven. A marketing-driven store is slick, focused on the offer and squeezing one more dollar; that's a dead end per Godin.
Shift to being market-driven: think about the hopes, dreams, and frustrations of your customers and their friends, and invest in changing the culture they live in.
When a tactic underperforms (a new logo, a data hack, a pricing model), ask whether the underlying product and promise match the market's worldview rather than patching the surface.
Route decisions back to what the market wants, not what you find easiest to sell. Being market-driven lasts; being marketing-driven doesn't.
caveats: This is Godin's opinion, not a measured rule; some stores may need marketing-driven execution to survive short-term.
Market-driven does not mean ignoring profitability—it means the customer's worldview leads.

cards.title: Find the lock before fashioning the key
cards.summary: Make products for customers you've identified rather than hunting for customers for products you already made.
cards.use_when: When choosing what to stock, design, or launch—product selection and range planning.
steps: Start from a specific group of people you want to serve, not from a product you already built.
Observe what that group already dreams of, believes, and wants, then design the product to fit them.
Resist reverse-engineering: don't invent a vague 'change' story to rationalize whatever you already sell.
Test the fit by asking whether people would pay you to produce the change you're promising.
caveats: Godin's framing assumes you have freedom to choose your market; established catalogs may need to work from existing inventory.

cards.title: Define the smallest viable market
cards.summary: Choose the minimum number of people you can delight and still make the effort worthwhile, then serve them obsessively.
cards.use_when: When deciding your target customer segment, niche, and initial launch audience instead of aiming at 'everyone'.
steps: Ask what's the smallest market you can survive on—for Union Square Cafe, founder Danny Meyer knew the dining room could serve only 600 people a day, so he curated which 600.
Choose the people most open to hearing your message and most likely to tell the right other people.
Search for a corner of the market that can't wait for your attention; overwhelm that group's wants and dreams with care and focus.
Once it works in that 'swimming pool,' find another swimming pool—or let your best customers spread the idea.
caveats: Specific is brave and accountable: you can measure whether it worked or spread.
Avoid the hubris of 'everyone'—mass means average and forces compromises that bore people.

cards.title: Segment by worldview (psychographics), not demographics
cards.summary: Group customers by the stories they tell themselves and what they believe, not by looks, because worldview predicts how they'll respond.
cards.use_when: When defining buyer personas for merchandising, ad targeting, and PDP messaging.
steps: List the beliefs, desires, and self-narratives that define your ideal customer, the way Starbucks served people with a precise set of beliefs about coffee, time, money, community, and luxury—distinct from Dunkin' customers.
Use example personas like Bargain Bill (shops as a sport, wrestles with money), Hurried Henry (wants shortcuts, won't read directions), Careful Karla (suspicious, avoids risk) to sharpen targeting.
Check whether each person has a problem, a desire, and a narrative—the three things every customer carries.
Beware assuming everyone is like you or wants what you want, as JCPenney's 2011 CEO did when he ended discounts and sales fell by more than 50 percent.
caveats: Typecasting is a deliberate simplification to serve better, not a claim about individuals.
Demographics can be useful but should not drive the core segmentation.

cards.title: Run five steps of marketing in order
cards.summary: Sequence: invent something worth making with a story worth telling, build it for a few people, tell the matching story to the smallest market, spread the word, then show up for years.
cards.use_when: When planning a new product launch or brand-building campaign and deciding what to do first.
steps: Invent a thing worth making, with a story worth telling and a contribution worth talking about.
Design and build it so that a few people will particularly benefit from and care about it.
Tell a story that matches the built-in narrative and dreams of that smallest viable market.
Only then do the spreading step that everyone gets excited about.
Finally, show up regularly, consistently, and generously for years to organize, lead, build confidence, and earn permission to follow up and teach.
caveats: Marketers tend to skip to step four (getting the word out), which Godin says is exactly backwards.
The sequence is recursive, and Godin says to backtrack, redo assumptions, and question existing practice.

cards.title: Make a three-sentence marketing promise
cards.summary: Write and use a template promise stating who the product is for, who you'll focus on, and what engaging with it helps them get.
cards.use_when: When writing brand positioning, homepage copy, PDP headlines, or ad creative that must make a clear promise.
steps: Fill the template: 'My product is for people who believe ___. I will focus on people who want ___. I promise that engaging with what I make will help you get ___.'
Ground the promise in the change you seek to make and the people you seek to change—not a slogan.
Note that a promise is not a guarantee; it's more like 'if this works for you, you're going to discover...'

Across contexts, map promised emotions to what people actually want: belonging, connection, peace of mind, status, respect, dominance, affiliation (e.g., 'They laughed when I sat down at the piano' promises status; 'Choosy mothers choose Jif' promises status and respect).
caveats: The promise may be hidden or camouflaged but all effective marketing makes one.
Do not overpromise; the promise should match the built-in narrative of your market.

cards.title: Sell the feeling, not the feature
cards.summary: People don't want your product; they want what it will do for them and how it will make them feel—extend the drill-bit insight to the final emotion.
cards.use_when: When writing product descriptions, benefit-led landing pages, and ad creative for any SKU.
steps: Extend Levitt's drill-bit idea: no one wants a quarter-inch hole; they want the shelf on the wall, the uncluttered room, the feeling of safety and respect.
Identify which desired emotion the product delivers—belonging, connection, peace of mind, status, or respect.
Write PDP and ad copy around the outcome and feeling, not around technical features.

Use the SUV example as a checklist: people buy Land Cruisers they never drive off-road and Teslas with unused Ludicrous Mode, so wouldn't utility be the primary driver? Don't assume it is for your category either.
Weigh the reality that most marketers deliver the same feelings through different products, services, and stories for different moments.
caveats: This is Godin's framing; utility still matters in many commodity categories.
Avoid inventing emotional benefits the product can't honestly support.

cards.title: Plan for the irrational, not the rational, customer
cards.summary: Assume people act on current irrational urges and cultural identity rather than weighing information and costs like a rational agent.
cards.use_when: When designing pricing, promotions, bundles, and checkout experiences that must account for real behavior.
steps: Don't assume the people you serve are well-informed, rational, independent, long-term choice makers.
Don't assume everyone is like you or knows what you know.
Instead bet that people act on current irrational urges, ignore contrary information, trade long term for short term, and are influenced by the culture they identify with.
Design offers and page flows that meet people where they are (identity, habit, urgency, emotion) rather than expecting them to compute optimal value.
caveats: Microeconomic rationality may appear on average across large groups but isn't something to bet on.
This is a heuristic about human behavior, not a license to manipulate.

cards.title: Set up market research trip like Penguin Magic
cards.summary: Build a specialist ecommerce experience with demonstration content, audience-specific insight, and customer reviews that cycle quality fast.
cards.use_when: When building a specialist store or category page and deciding what content and social proof to include.
steps: Use video demonstrations for every product, showing the result without revealing the secret—creating tension that drives purchase (Penguin Magic's videos have been viewed over a billion times at no distribution cost).

Identify a structural insight about your audience: Penguin realized professional magicians rarely buy new tricks while amateurs with the same audience are hooked on changing routines—serving the amateurs who buy repeatedly.
Collect in-depth reviews from fellow practitioners, not generic review-site commenters (Penguin has 82,000+ product reviews), which makes your stock quality cycle rapidly.
Invest in community: Penguin hosts 300 lectures and nearly 100 live conventions, and maintains an email list of tens of thousands of customers.
Compete by being very different from Amazon, not by trying to be the Amazon of your category.
caveats: The billion views and 82,000 reviews are case-study figures, not promises for other stores.
Specialist depth requires genuine category expertise.

cards.title: Use anticipation, personalization, and relevance to earn permission
cards.summary: Own a direct-contact permission asset—email—and earn the right to reach people without a middleman by making every message anticipated, personal, and relevant.
cards.use_when: When building and sending email lists, newsletters, and lifecycle campaigns; not for blast tactics.
steps: Treat your list as a valuable owned asset: never spam, rent, or sell it, and never buy lists.
Set the strict permission bar: communicate only with 'people who would miss you if you didn't reach out.'
Deliver on the exact promise made during enrollment and communicate drip by drip.
Move from acting as a 'sharecropper' on rented social media land to owning direct-contact permission.
Make every send anticipated, personal, and relevant so it's welcome rather than an interruption.
caveats: Permission is a baseline requirement, not optional—skip spam and interrupt-stranger tactics entirely.
Owning a list means consistent, years-long generosity, not one-off campaigns.

cards.title: Create tension and relieve it at each step of the journey
cards.summary: Use tension deliberately—like the un-young-explained magic trick—and relieve it as customers progress toward their goal.
cards.use_when: When structuring PDP flow, upsells, content sequences, and onboarding to keep people moving.
steps: Identify the emotional tension at each stage of the customer's journey toward their goal.
Create tension where it motivates action (e.g., showing the outcome without revealing how, as Penguin Magic does with tricks).
Relieve tension at each step so progress feels satisfying rather than frustrating.
Do this as a 'show up often, with humility, focusing on the parts that work' habit, as in the Open Heart Project's eight principles.
caveats: Tension is a technique, not license to mislead; the relief must be real and delivered.
Too much unresolved tension creates frustration and abandonment.

cards.title: Design for loss aversion instead of the desire for gain
cards.summary: Frame the offer as keeping what they already have rather than shopping for something new, which can roughly double conversion in low-trust or low-income contexts.
cards.use_when: When structuring offers, trials, samples, or checkout for audiences that see buying as risk rather than fun.
steps: Run the VisionSpring test: show the working product first, then offer the choice.
Change the transaction from 'here's an opportunity to shop and choose' to 'here are your new glasses—if they work and you like them, pay; if not, give them back.'
Note the result: this single change roughly doubled the percentage of glasses sold, from about one third who bought when choosing from ten styles off the table.
Diagnose whether your audience experiences shopping as a fun risk (suburban mall teenagers) or as a threat (people living in poverty), and frame accordingly.
caveats: This is a case-study result from a specific village context, not a universal conversion benchmark.
The technique assumes you can deliver and reverse the transaction without abuse.

cards.title: Choose a market-driven change and avoid two common stumbles
cards.summary: Define the specific change you're making happen, then avoid grandiosity and reverse-engineered buzzword change definitions.
cards.use_when: When writing your brand mission, category positioning, or campaign brief and deciding what change you're making.
steps: Own that you're in the business of making change happen rather than hiding behind the product as the only deliverable.
Avoid stumble one: picking a grandiose, nearly impossible change you can't resource; instead start with a hurdle you can leap, then replicate the process on bigger challenges.

Avoid stumble two: reverse-engineering a 'change' to defend whatever you already sell, loaded with meaningless buzzwords (Godin cites 'Activation and engagement for TNT's new thriller that makes a meta-statement about viewer identity').
Write it concretely, as By the Way Bakery does: 'We want to make sure no one is left out... we change hosts from exclusive to inclusive, and guests from outsiders to insiders.'
caveats: Change can be trivial (1% market share shift) or profound, but the definition must be specific and real.
A vague mission fails because it gives you a convenient excuse in moments of despair.

cards.title: Use 'it's not for you' to filter and focus
cards.summary: Respectfully telling some people the product isn't for them sharpens your work for the people it is for—and protects your story from nonbelievers.
cards.use_when: When writing brand copy, choosing who to target in ads, and deciding how to handle critical reviews.
steps: Accept that every best-selling book on Amazon has at least a few one-star reviews; work that matters can't please everyone.
Use the comedian's dilemma: a comic bombing in New York may simply be performing for an Italian tour group who don't understand English—maybe the work failed, or maybe it wasn't clear who it was for.
Instead of sanding off the edges to fit the mass audience, keep your focus on the smallest viable audience you originally set out to serve.
Apply it in practice: say 'I made this for you. Not for the other folks, but for you.'
caveats: The source's framing is that respecting someone means not wasting their time pandering to them.
Distinguish 'not for you' from dismissing legitimate product-quality problems.

cards.title: Substitute 'students' for 'prospects and customers'
cards.summary: Reframe buyers as students you enroll and educate, shifting from a power dynamic of compliance to one of enrollment, choice, and care.
cards.use_when: When designing onboarding emails, content marketing, tutorials, and retention touchpoints.
steps: Replace 'prospects' and 'customers' with 'students' in your internal framing.
Ask: where are your students? What will they benefit from learning? Are they open to being taught? What will they tell others?
Adopt the student–mentor relationship of enrollment, choice, and care—not the student–teacher relationship of testing and compliance.
Ask yourself what you'd want to be taught and what you'd teach if given the chance.
caveats: This is a reframing device, not a claim that customers want to be lectured.
Keep the emphasis on enrollment and mutual choice.

cards.title: Apply the Open Heart Project's eight-part growth system
cards.summary: Build a community by starting from real empathy, serving the smallest viable market, matching worldview, making it easy to spread, keeping attention, offering depth, creating and relieving tension, and showing up often.
cards.use_when: When growing a subscription, membership, or community-driven store and deciding how to deepen customer relationships.
steps: Start with empathy to see a real need: not 'how can I start a business?' but 'what would matter here?'
Focus on the smallest viable market: how few people could find this indispensable and still make it worth doing?
Match the worldview of the people being served—tell the story they want to hear in language they're eager to understand.
Make it easy to spread: if every member brings one more, within a few years you'll have more members than you can count.
Earn and keep attention and trust; offer ways to go deeper; instead of looking for members for your work, do work for your members.
At every step, create and relieve tension as people progress toward their goals; show up often with humility, focusing on the parts that work.
caveats: The 20,000-member result and one-person staff are case-study specifics, not guarantees.
Membership depth requires ongoing content and connection.

cards.title: Build a generous beacon, not a selfish USP
cards.summary: Find a spot on the map with edges that some people want, and signal it clearly, rather than maximizing market share with a narrow unique selling proposition.
cards.use_when: When defining your brand's differentiating position and best-for claim in a crowded category.
steps: Accept that 'better' isn't transitive for subjective categories: an Hermès bag is more expensive than Louis Vuitton, but that doesn't make it 'better' in any absolute sense.

Work out who remembers your brand as the best for what: someone who cares about sustainability and price has a slot for their favorite brand, and their neighbor who cares about status and luxury has a different one.
Send up a signal flare, a generous beacon, so people looking for you can find you easily.
Frame everything as 'we're this, not that,' rather than a self-serving USP.
caveats: Better isn't up to you; taste matters and everyone else may disagree.
Expense and similar measurable attributes aren't always the dimensions people care about.

cards.title: Use storytelling, connection, and experience as core tools
cards.summary: Stories, connections, and experiences are timeless marketing tools that build trust and belonging more durably than any shiny digital shortcut.
cards.use_when: When planning content, community, and post-purchase experience instead of chasing new channel tactics.
steps: Tell true stories made true by your actions, products, and services, so they hold up over time.
Make connections: humans are lonely and want to be seen and known, and want to be part of something safer and more fun.
Create experiences with intent—using a product, engaging with a service, calling customer service, going to a rally—each action is part of the story and builds connection.
Treat marketing as all of it: what you make, how you make it, and who you make it for, and the effects and side effects, the pricing and profit, all at once.
caveats: Stories must be true, made true by actions, not inflated claims.
This requires organizational buy-in because marketing is everyone's job.

cards.title: Recognize that marketing shifts from ads to empathy in a world of tiny whispers
cards.summary: The internet is the first mass medium not built for interruption, so effective marketing relies on empathy and service rather than buying attention.
cards.use_when: When allocating budget between paid interruption ads and building a brand that earns discovery, trust, and spread.
steps: Recognize that TV and radio were built to hold ads, but the internet is a billion tiny whispers—selfish conversations that rarely include you.
Stop assuming you can steal attention cheaply the way previous generations did with mass media.
Instead of asking 'how do I get the word out?' first, do the other part first: understand the customer's worldview and desires so you can connect.
Spend on getting discovered last, not first; see what others see, build tension, align with tribes, and create ideas that spread.
caveats: This is Godin's directional claim about media change, not a blanket ban on all paid advertising.
Paid acquisition can still work; it's just no longer the reliable default it once was.

cards.title: Wait for better is not selling with a rational argument
cards.summary: Better is relative to what a specific person cares about, so frame your offer as better for those who share your market's values, not objectively superior.
cards.use_when: When crafting comparison claims, product superiority messaging, and promotional copy.
steps: Accept that when a marketer says 'this is better,' they actually mean 'this is better for someone and it might be better for you.'
Identify which dimension matters to your segment (sustainability, price, status, taste), and claim that dimension rather than a vague superiority.
Note the Beer Advocate case: 250 beers have earned 3,400+ ratings each, and each is someone's favorite—taste matters and everyone else can be wrong.
Avoid linear A > B > C reasoning on subjective attributes like stylish or fashionable.
caveats: Expense is easy to measure but more of it isn't always better.
Claims of superiority in your segment are not universal truths.

cards.title: Treat every purchase as a bargain the buyer thinks they're getting
cards.summary: People buy when they believe what they get is worth more than what they pay—so withholding options is a kind of theft from the buyer's narrative.
cards.use_when: When setting prices and constructing offers, and when writing nonprofit, donation, or premium pricing pages.
steps: Use the nonprofit fundraising example: if the fundraiser thinks a $1M ask is crazy based on her own worldview, the donation won't happen; the donation is for the donor, who gets $2M worth of joy, status, and satisfaction, and that's fine.
Accept that everything we purchase is a bargain—we bought it because it was worth more than we paid.
If you're unwilling to have empathy for the narrative of the person you seek to serve, you're withholding a valuable option.
If they understand the offer and decline, that's okay—it's not for them today, not at this price, not with that structure.
caveats: Empathy for the buyer's narrative is not the same as overpricing or manipulation.
A declined offer is not always a failure of the seller.

cards.title: Market to the human condition as Godin defines it
cards.summary: Everyone has a rich internal life, thinks they're right, is afraid and lonely and insecure, and cares about something—so empathy is the heart of marketing.
cards.use_when: When researching customer motivations, writing brand voice guidelines, and designing experiences for return customers.
steps: Internalize sonder: everyone around you has an internal life as rich and conflicted as yours.

Assume everyone thinks they are right, has suffered affronts, is afraid, feels lucky, wants to contribute, wants things they can't have, is lonely, insecure, and a bit of a fraud—and cares about something.
Stop trying to do marketing 'to' people by insisting they get with your program; dance with them instead.
Use this to design offers that meet people where they actually are.
caveats: This is Godin's characterization of the human condition, not a research finding.
Avoid overgeneralizing from it to override specific customer research.

why: Defines email marketing not as blasting spam, but as managing a closely guarded permission asset built on anticipated, consensual, and relevant communication.

scope_hint: baseline

Topics. permission acquisition / earning the right to contact people without a middleman; list management / treating the list as a valuable asset and never spamming, renting, or selling it; engagement / delivering on the exact promise made during enrollment and communicating drip by drip. Look for. The strict definition of permission: communicating only with "people who would miss you if you didn't reach out". The strategic transition from acting as a "sharecropper" on rented social media land to owning a direct-contact permission asset. Skip. Spam tactics, purchasing email lists, or strategies relying on interrupting strangers without enrollment. Scope mix. 100% baseline (permission is a mandatory requirement for lifecycle marketing). Volume. 200 to 300.

Marketing has changed, but our understanding of what we’re supposed to do next hasn’t kept up. When in doubt, we selfishly shout. When in a corner, we play small ball, stealing from our competition instead of broadening the market. When pressed, we assume that everyone is just like us, but uninformed. Mostly, we remember growing up in a mass market world, where TV and the Top 40 hits defined us. As marketers, we seek to repeat the old-fashioned tricks that don’t work anymore. The compass points toward trust Every three hundred thousand years or so, the north pole and the south pole switch places. The magnetic fields of the Earth flip. In our culture, it happens more often than that. And in the world of culture change, it just happened. The true north, the method that works best, has flipped. Instead of selfish mass, effective marketing now relies on empathy and service. In this book, we’re working together to solve a set of related problems. How to spread your ideas. How to make the impact you seek. How to improve the culture. There isn’t an obvious road map. No simple step-by-step series of tactics. But what I can promise you is a compass: a true north. A recursive method that will get better the more you use it. This book is based on a hundred-day seminar, one that involves not just lessons but peer-to-peer coaching around shared work. In TheMarketingSeminar.com we assemble thousands of marketers and challenge them to go deeper, to share their journey, to challenge each other to see what truly works. As you read through, don’t hesitate to backtrack, to redo an assumption, to As you read through, don’t hesitate to backtrack, to redo an assumption, to question an existing practice—you can adjust, test, measure, and repeat. Marketing is one of our greatest callings. It’s the work of positive change. I’m thrilled that you’re on this journey, and I hope you’ll find the tools you need here. Marketing is not a battle, and it’s not a war, or even a contest Marketing is the generous act of helping someone solve a problem. Their problem. It’s a chance to change the culture for the better. Marketing involves very little in the way of shouting, hustling, or coercion. It’s a chance to serve, instead. The internet is the first mass medium that wasn’t invented to make marketers happy. Television was invented to hold TV ads, and radio was invented to give radio ads a place to live. But the internet isn’t built around interruption and mass. It’s the largest medium, but it’s also the smallest one. There’s no mass, and you can’t steal attention for a penny the way your grandparents’ companies did. To be really clear: the internet feels like a vast, free media playground, a place where all your ideas deserve to be seen by just about everyone. In fact, it’s a billion tiny whispers, an endless series of selfish conversations that rarely include you or the work you do. The magic of ads is a trap that keeps us from building a useful story For a long time, the most efficient way for a commercial enterprise to make large-scale change was simple: buy ads. Ads worked. Ads were a bargain. Ads paid for themselves. Besides, they were fun to make. You could buy a lot all at once. They made you (or your brand) a little famous. And they were reliable: money spent equaled sales made. Is it any wonder that, pretty quickly, marketers decided that advertising was what they did? For most of my lifetime, marketing was advertising. And then it wasn’t true anymore. Which means you’ll need to become a marketer instead. That means seeing what others see. Building tension. Aligning with tribes. Creating ideas that spread. It means doing the hard work of becoming driven by the market and working with (your part of) that market. On getting the word out (precisely the wrong question) “How do I get the word out?” The SEO expert promises that you will be found when people search for you. The Facebook consultant tells you how to interrupt just the right people. The PR professional promises articles and mentions and profiles. And Don Draper, David Ogilvy, and the rest will trade your money for ads. Beautiful, sexy, effective ads. All to get the word out. But that’s not marketing, not anymore. And it doesn’t work, not anymore. We’re going to talk about how you’ll be discovered. But it’s the last part, not the first. Marketing is important enough to do right, which means doing the other part first. Shameless marketers brought shame to the rest of us A short-term, profit-maximizing hustler can easily adopt a shameless mind-set. Spamming, tricking, coercing. Is there any other profession that proudly does this? You won’t find civil engineers who call senior citizens in the middle of the night to sell them worthless collectible coins. You won’t hear of accountants who extract customers’ data without permission, or orchestra conductors who proudly post fake reviews online. This shameless pursuit of attention at the expense of the truth has driven many ethical and generous marketers to hide their best work, to feel shame about the prospect of being market-driven. That’s not okay. The other kind of marketing, the effective kind, is about understanding our customers’ worldview and desires so we can connect with them. It’s focused on being missed when you’re gone, on bringing more than people expect to those who trust us. It seeks volunteers, not victims. There’s a groundswell of people doing marketing because they know they can make things better. They’re prepared to engage with the market because they know they can contribute to our culture. People like you. People like you. The lock and the key It doesn’t make any sense to make a key and then run around looking for a lock to open. The only productive solution is to find a lock and then fashion a key. It’s easier to make products and services for the customers you seek to serve than it is to find customers for your products and services. Marketing doesn’t have to be selfish In fact, the best marketing never is. Marketing is the generous act of helping others become who they seek to become. It involves creating honest stories—stories that resonate and spread. Marketers offer solutions, opportunities for humans to solve their problems and move forward. And when our ideas spread, we change the culture. We build something that people would miss if it were gone, something that gives them meaning, connection, and possibility. The other kind of marketing—the hype, scams, and pressure—thrives on selfishness. I know that it doesn’t work in the long run, and that you can do better than that. We all can. Case Study: Penguin Magic Hocus has left the building. Penguin Magic is the sort of company that they invented the internet for. You may have grown up near a magic shop. There’s still one in my little town. Dimly lit, with fake wood paneling, almost certainly with the owner manning the counter. While he may have loved the work, he certainly wasn’t very successful. Today, if you care about magic, you know about Penguin Magic. It’s not the Amazon of magic tricks (because being the Amazon of anything is difficult indeed). Instead, it has grown to significant size by being very different from Amazon and by understanding precisely what its audience wants, knows, and believes. First, every trick for sale on the site is demonstrated with a video. That video, First, every trick for sale on the site is demonstrated with a video. That video, of course, doesn’t reveal how the trick is done, so tension is created. If you want to know the secret, you’ll need to buy the trick. To date, their videos, on the site and on YouTube, have been seen more than a billion times. A billion views with no cost of distribution. Second, the people who run the site realized that professional magicians rarely buy tricks, because they only need ten or twenty regular tricks in their bag. Since the audience changes every night, they don’t worry about repeating themselves. An amateur, on the other hand, always has the same audience (friends and family) and so he’s hooked on constantly changing the routine. Third, every trick is reviewed in detail. Not reviewed by the knuckleheads who hang out on Yelp or Amazon, but reviewed by other magicians. It’s a tough crowd, but one that appreciates good work. There are more than eighty-two thousand product reviews on the site. As a result, the quality of stock on Penguin cycles very rapidly. Creators see their competitors’ work immediately, giving them an impetus to make something even better. Instead of a production cycle measured in years, it might take only a month for an idea to go from notion to product on Penguin. To date, they’ve carried more than sixteen thousand different items on their site. Going forward, Penguin continues to invest in building connections not just with the community (they have an email list of tens of thousands of customers) but across it as well. They’ve hosted three hundred lectures, which have become the TED Talks of magic, as well as going into the field and running nearly a hundred live conventions. The more magicians learn from each other, the more likely that Penguin will do well. You’re not a cigar-smoking fat cat You don’t work for a soap company. You’re not an obsolete industrial marketer. So why are you acting like one? Your Kickstarter is nearing its deadline, so sure, you have a good excuse to spam every “influencer” you know, begging for a link. But they ignore you. You work for a content marketing company, and you obsessively track how many clicks your articles get, even though the crap you write embarrasses you. You make graphs of how many Instagram followers you have, even though you know everyone else simply buys followers. you know everyone else simply buys followers. You lower your price because people tell you your rates are too high, but it doesn’t seem to help. It’s all the same old thing—the industrialized selfish same-old, made modern for a new generation. Your emergency is not a license to steal my attention. Your insecurity is not a permit to hustle me or my friends. There’s a more effective way. You can do it. It’s not easy, but the steps are well lit. It’s time Time to get off the social media merry-go-round that goes faster and faster but never gets anywhere. Time to stop hustling and interrupting. Time to stop spamming and pretending you’re welcome. Time to stop making average stuff for average people while hoping you can charge more than a commodity price. Time to stop begging people to become your clients, and time to stop feeling bad about charging for your work. Time to stop looking for shortcuts, and time to start insisting on a long, viable path instead. CHAPTER TWO The Marketer Learns to See In 1983, I was a very young and inexperienced brand manager at Spinnaker, the startup software company I joined after business school. Suddenly, I had millions of dollars in my budget, fancy lunches with ad reps that I didn’t ask for, and an urgent need: to get the word out about the software my amazing team had created. I wasted all that ad money. The ads didn’t work because the ads were ignored. Somehow, though, the software sold. Over the years, I’ve launched dozens and dozens of projects and sold goods and services to businesses and individuals. I’ve worked with Jay Levinson, the father of Guerrilla Marketing, with Lester Wunderman, the godfather of direct mail, and Bernadette Jiwa, the doyenne of storytelling. My ideas have built billion-dollar companies and raised nearly that much for important charities. Mostly, the journey has involved noticing what works and trying to understand what doesn’t. It’s been an ongoing experiment of trial and error (mostly error) with projects and organizations I care about. And now I have a compass for what marketing is today, about the human condition, and about our culture. This approach is simple, but it’s not easy to embrace, because it involves patience, empathy, and respect. The marketing that has suffused our entire lives is not the marketing that you want to do. The shortcuts using money to buy attention to sell average stuff to average people are an artifact of another time, not the one we live in now. You can learn to see how human beings dream, decide, and act. And if you help them become better versions of themselves, the ones they seek to be, you’re a marketer. Marketing in five steps The first step is to invent a thing worth making, with a story worth telling, and a contribution worth talking about. The second step is to design and build it in a way that a few people will particularly benefit from and care about. The third step is to tell a story that matches the built-in narrative and dreams of that tiny group of people, the smallest viable market. The fourth step is the one everyone gets excited about: spread the word. The last step is often overlooked: show up—regularly, consistently, and generously, for years and years—to organize and lead and build confidence in the change you seek to make. To earn permission to follow up and to earn enrollment to teach. As marketers, we get to consistently do the work to help the idea spread from person to person, engaging a tribe as you make change happen. This Is Marketing: An executive summary Ideas that spread, win. Marketers make change happen: for the smallest viable market, and by delivering anticipated, personal, and relevant messages that people actually want to get. Marketers don’t use consumers to solve their company’s problem; they use marketing to solve other people’s problems. They have the empathy to know that those they seek to serve don’t want what the marketer wants, don’t believe what they believe, and don’t care about what they care about. They probably never will. At the heart of our culture is our belief in status, in our self-perceived understanding of our role in any interaction, in where we’re going next. We use status roles and our decisions about affiliation and dominion to decide where to go and how to get there. Persistent, consistent, and frequent stories, delivered to an aligned audience, will earn attention, trust, and action. Direct marketing is not the same as brand marketing, but they are both based on our decision to make the right thing for the right people. “People like us do things like this” is how each of us understands culture, and marketers engage with this idea every day. Ideas move through a slope. They skate through the early adopters, leap through a chasm, and slog their way to the masses. Sometimes. Attention is a precious resource since our brains are cluttered with noise. Attention is a precious resource since our brains are cluttered with noise. Smart marketers make it easy for those they seek to work with, by helping position the offering in a way that resonates and is memorable. Most of all, marketing begins (and often ends) with what we do and how we do it, not in all the stuff that comes after the thing is designed and shipped. Your tactics can make a difference, but your strategy—your commitment to a way of being and a story to be told and a promise to be made—can change everything. If you want to make change, begin by making culture. Begin by organizing a tightly knit group. Begin by getting people in sync. Culture beats strategy—so much that culture is strategy. Things marketers know 1. Committed, creative people can change the world (in fact, they’re the only ones who do). You can do it right now, and you can make more change than you can possibly imagine. 2. You cannot change everyone; therefore, asking, “Who’s it for?” can focus your actions and help you deal with the nonbelievers (in your head and in the outside world). 3. Change is best made with intent. “What’s it for?” is the posture of work that matters. 4. Human beings tell themselves stories. Those stories, as far as each of us is concerned, are completely and totally true, and it’s foolish to try to persuade them (or us) otherwise. 5. We can group people into stereotyped groups that often (but not always) tell themselves similar stories, groups that make similar decisions based on their perceived status and other needs. 6. What you say isn’t nearly as important as what others say about you. CHAPTER THREE Marketing Changes People Through Stories, Connections, and Experience Case Study: VisionSpring—Selling glasses to people who need them Each person has a story in his or her head, a narrative used to navigate the world. The extraordinary thing is that every person’s narrative is different. A few years ago, I went with a small team to a village in India, trying to understand the challenges that VisionSpring faces in their work. VisionSpring is a social enterprise that works to get reading glasses to the billion people around the world who need them but don’t have them. When the typical person only lived to thirty or forty years of age, it didn’t matter that most people will need reading glasses beginning at age fifty. But as lifespans have increased, more and more people find themselves otherwise healthy and active but unable to work—because they can’t read or do close-up work. If you’re a weaver or a jeweler or a nurse, working without glasses can be impossible. VisionSpring’s strategy is to produce attractive glasses in bulk at a very low cost, perhaps two dollars a pair. And then, working with local traveling salespeople, they bring the glasses to villages around the world, where they sell them for three dollars or so a pair. The one-dollar difference between the manufacturing cost and the price is just enough to pay for shipping, for local talent, and for the organization to keep growing. When we set up our table in the village, many people came to see what was going on. It was the middle of a very hot day and there wasn’t much else to do. Thinking about “better” It’s tempting to decide that there’s a transitive relationship, that A > B > C. This works, for example, with length. A ruler is longer than a thumb and a thumb is longer than a peppercorn, and therefore a ruler is longer than a peppercorn. But linear comparisons don’t make sense when we’re building stories and opportunities for humans. An Hermès bag is more expensive than a Louis Vuitton bag, which is more expensive than one from Coach. But that doesn’t mean that the Hermès bag is “better.” It merely means that it’s more expensive, which is just one of the many things that someone might care about. Expense might be easy to measure, but it’s never clear that more of it is always better. What about more subjective categories like “stylish” or “fashionable” or “status”? Suddenly, it’s not linear. Not easy to measure. Not clear at all what better means. Better isn’t up to you There are more than 250 models of motorcycles available for sale in Cleveland. Can you name them? No one can, not even a motorcycle collector. And the same thing is true for ketchup, for insurance brokers, for churches. So, how do we process this, remember this, choose a product? We remember the best one. Best for what? And that’s the key question. Best for us. If we care about sustainability and price, then our brain has a slot for our favorite brand, and it’s the one that’s the best at sustainability and price. No surprise. But our neighbor, the one who cares far more about status within the group and luxury, has a very different brand in mind. Which is not surprising, because we’re humans, not machines. Your job as a marketer is to find a spot on the map with edges that (some) people want to find. Not a selfish, unique selling proposition, done to maximize your market share, but a generous beacon, a signal flare sent up so that people who are looking for you can easily find you. We have no clue whether dogs enjoy it more, because we’re not dogs. But we can be sure that dog owners like it more. Because dog food is for dog owners. It’s for the way it makes them feel, the satisfaction of taking care of an animal that responds with loyalty and affection, the status of buying a luxury good, and the generosity of sharing it.
